analysis.one_liner: Requires binding arbitration when a new union and employer can't agree on a first contract.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee and a subcommittee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When workers vote to form a union, the employer and union must negotiate a first contract. This bill would set a deadline: after 120 days of negotiation without agreement, a mediator would be brought in, and if that failed, a binding arbitrator would decide the contract terms. Employers would no longer be able to stall a first contract indefinitely. The bill never moved past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at newly organized workplaces, who would get an enforceable first contract instead of waiting months or years while an employer bargains in bad faith or slow-walks the process. Unions also gain, because a guaranteed first contract makes organizing more likely to pay off.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the employer and the new union to select a mediator within 60 days of union certification if they have not reached a contract, with the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service choosing one if they cannot agree [S3].
If mediation fails within 30 days, either party can send the remaining disputes to binding arbitration, meaning an arbitrator imposes a final contract either side must accept [S3].
The CRS summary states the bill amends the National Labor Relations Act to require mediation and, if necessary, binding arbitration of initial contract negotiation disputes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would lose their most effective tool for weakening a newly formed union: refusing to agree on a first contract so the union has no enforceable deal. Some of the cost would show up in contract terms set by arbitrators rather than by voluntary agreement.

drawbacks.text: A binding arbitrator, not the workers or the employer, would set the final contract terms, which means a contract nobody at the table actually negotiated [S3].

Critics of mandatory first-contract arbitration argue it weakens genuine collective bargaining by giving one side an exit to a third-party decision instead of an incentive to compromise; this objection was not resolved in any hearing because the bill never received one [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real, documented problem: newly certified unions can be strangled by an employer's refusal to agree to a first contract, and current law offers no remedy beyond years of litigation. Binding arbitration solves the delay but replaces bargaining with a third party's decision, and the imposed contract may fit the workplace worse than a negotiated one. It is a blunt fix to a genuine imbalance, and it died without any hearing where its design could have been tested or improved.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 7, 2009 by Rep. Gene Green of Texas and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S5].

On March 16, 2009 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, and it never received a hearing, a markup, a vote, or floor action for the rest of the 111th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who prefer to stall or exhaust newly formed unions keep the ability to delay a first contract indefinitely without facing binding arbitration. New unions and the workers who vote for them remain exposed to that delay strategy.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill's referral to subcommittee was the last action ever taken

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill attracted no cosponsors from either party, so the partisan split was never recorded; it was introduced by a moderate Democrat in a Democratic-controlled Congress that also declined to act on it.

industries.note: The bill would force a first contract within roughly 120 days through mediation and binding arbitration, removing the option of stalling indefinitely. Employers' interest in avoiding imposed contracts runs directly against workers' interest in getting an enforceable deal.
A guaranteed path to a first contract makes union representation worth more to workers and makes organizing campaigns more likely to succeed.
